steps: Check deploy history: run `kubectl rollout history deployment/api-gateway` to list recent deploys
Identify the most recent deploy timestamp and correlate with the alert onset time
Review the deploy diff: check commit in GitHub at https://github.com/acme-corp/api-gateway/commits
Look for changes to middleware, config loading, or environment variable reads
If culprit deploy identified within the last 2 hours, initiate rollback: `kubectl rollout undo deployment/api-gateway`
Monitor error_rate metric for 5 minutes post-rollback to confirm recovery
If rollback does not resolve, escalate to #oncall-platform with deploy ID and timeline
Check which upstream dependency is causing failures: inspect gateway logs for upstream error messages
Verify auth-service health: `curl -s http://auth-service/health/live`
Verify user-service health: `curl -s http://user-service/health/live`
If auth-service is slow (latency cascade): check auth-service logs for slow queries or thread pool exhaustion
If a downstream service is degraded, consider enabling circuit breaker bypass for non-critical routes
Escalate to the owning team's oncall channel with the specific failing upstream dependency
Document impact scope: how many routes are affected and what percentage of user traffic
Check for recent ConfigMap changes: `kubectl describe configmap api-gateway-config`
Compare with previous config version in git: https://github.com/acme-corp/api-gateway/blob/main/k8s/configmap.yaml
Identify the changed config key and correlate with error pattern in logs
If a feature flag was recently toggled, check the flag state and disable it via config management
Rollback ConfigMap to previous version: `kubectl apply -f k8s/configmap.yaml` (from previous commit)
Restart pods to reload config: `kubectl rollout restart deployment/api-gateway`
Verify error rate returns to baseline within 5 minutes
Check recent deploys: `kubectl rollout history deployment/user-service`
Correlate most recent deploy timestamp with error onset in logs
Review commit diff at https://github.com/acme-corp/user-service/commits — focus on dependency changes (requirements.txt) and DB query code
Check for library version upgrades that may have breaking API changes
If dependency version bump is the likely cause, initiate rollback: `kubectl rollout undo deployment/user-service`
Check for DB migration issues: `python manage.py showmigrations` to verify no pending or failed migrations
Monitor user-service error_rate for 5 minutes post-rollback
Check connection pool utilization: look for 'pool at capacity' or 'connection pool exhausted' in logs
Identify the query holding connections: search logs for 'slow query' or 'full table scan' entries
Check for recent batch jobs or cron tasks that may have added DB load
If a recent deploy introduced new queries: `kubectl rollout undo deployment/user-service`
Temporary mitigation: scale up DB connection pool limit in config and restart pods
Add missing index if identified: coordinate with team-identity for hotfix deploy
After resolution, add query to slow query monitoring alerts
Check for recent feature flag changes in the config store
Look for partial failure pattern: ~50% error rates often indicate a flag rollout to a subset of users
Identify the flag by correlating log errors with flag assignment metadata
Disable the suspect feature flag: set rollout percentage to 0% in config management
Verify error rate drops to baseline within 2 minutes of flag disable
Notify feature owner in #oncall-identity with the flag name and bug description
Do not re-enable the flag until the underlying code bug is fixed and tested
Check recent auth-service deploys: `kubectl rollout history deployment/auth-service`
Look for errors referencing missing env vars (KeyError) or missing config keys — check startup logs
If KeyError on env var: check the Kubernetes Secret and ConfigMap for the missing key
Add missing secret: `kubectl create secret generic auth-secrets --from-literal=OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET=<value>`
If adding the secret is not immediately possible, rollback: `kubectl rollout undo deployment/auth-service`
Verify api-gateway can reach auth-service after rollback: check gateway error rate
Document the missing config key and add it to the deployment checklist for future releases
Check if auth-service itself is healthy: `curl -s http://auth-service/health/live`
If auth-service is slow (high latency), check for slow DB queries in logs
Look for 'full table scan' or 'Seq scan' entries in logs — may indicate a missing index
If a recent deploy introduced a new DB query, rollback: `kubectl rollout undo deployment/auth-service`
As a temporary mitigation, add a DB index: `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_sessions_user_id ON sessions(user_id);`
Check that user-service is also healthy (auth-service depends on it for user lookup)
Alert api-gateway team (#oncall-platform) as they will see cascading latency
Check recent deploys: `kubectl rollout history deployment/payment-service`
IMPORTANT: Payment service changes require security review — do not rollback without notifying #oncall-payments
Identify the failing code path in logs — look for exception type and stack trace
If the deploy modified Stripe client configuration or API version, rollback immediately
Rollback: `kubectl rollout undo deployment/payment-service`
Verify Stripe webhook delivery is not affected: check Stripe dashboard for webhook errors
Post-incident: create a security review task for the offending deploy before re-merging
Check DB connection pool utilization in logs: look for 'pool at capacity' or timeout errors
Identify if exhaustion is traffic-driven (spike) or leak-driven (gradual over hours)
For traffic spike: scale payment-service pods — `kubectl scale deployment/payment-service --replicas=6`
For connection leak: identify the leaking query or batch job in recent deploys
Check for slow queries: look for 'full table scan' on payment_records table
Add missing index as hotfix: coordinate with team-payments for immediate deploy
Monitor pool utilization after scaling — if still exhausting, escalate to team-payments
Check internal payment-service health: `curl -s http://payment-service/health/live` — if healthy, the issue is external
Check Stripe status page: https://status.stripe.com — look for active incidents
Verify Stripe API connectivity: look for 'HTTP 503 from api.stripe.com' in logs
If Stripe is down: escalate to account manager and activate fallback processor (Adyen) per runbook rb-payment-service-fallback
Notify order-service team (#oncall-commerce) — they will see order creation failures
Post status update to #incidents: 'Payment processing unavailable due to Stripe outage — ETA per Stripe status page'
Do NOT attempt rollbacks — this is an external dependency issue, not a code issue
Check recent deploys: `kubectl rollout history deployment/order-service`
Correlate deploy timestamp with error onset — look for <15 minute gap
Review commit diff for changes to order creation, DB queries, or external service calls
Check if batch jobs were introduced or modified in this deploy
If batch job changes are present, check for resource leak patterns in logs (connection pool, memory)
Rollback: `kubectl rollout undo deployment/order-service`
Verify payment-service and notification-service downstream traffic normalizes after rollback
Check connection pool utilization trend: is it rising gradually (leak) or sudden (spike)?
For gradual leak: search logs for 'cursor not closed', 'connection not returned to pool', or similar warnings
Identify the leaking code path — typically a try/finally block missing cursor.close()
Check if a recent deploy introduced batch jobs or new DB query code
Immediate mitigation: restart the deployment to flush leaked connections: `kubectl rollout restart deployment/order-service`
For a hotfix: the fix is adding cursor.close() in the finally block of the offending method
After hotfix deploy, monitor pool utilization over 3 hours to confirm the leak is stopped
Check recent deploys: `kubectl rollout history deployment/notification-service`
Review commit for changes to WebSocket handlers, event emitters, or connection lifecycle code
If WebSocket changes: check for EventEmitter maxListeners warnings in logs — indicates listener leak
If memory is growing gradually post-deploy: this is likely a listener/resource leak
Rollback: `kubectl rollout undo deployment/notification-service`
Verify pod memory stabilizes after rollback — should stop growing within 30 minutes
The fix for listener leaks: ensure emitter.off() is called on disconnect in a finally/cleanup handler
Check memory trend in logs: is growth sudden (bad deploy) or gradual over hours (leak)?
Look for 'EventEmitter: possible memory leak' warnings — indicates listener accumulation
Check WebSocket connection handling code in the most recent deploy
If pod is in CrashLoopBackOff: `kubectl describe pod <pod>` to check OOM kill reason
Immediate mitigation: rollback to previous version — `kubectl rollout undo deployment/notification-service`
Confirm by checking if memory stabilizes at baseline (~250MB) after rollback
Root fix: ensure cleanup handlers call emitter.removeAllListeners() or emitter.off() on disconnect
Note: analytics-pipeline is best-effort tier — user-facing services are not blocked by this service
Check recent deploys: `kubectl rollout history deployment/analytics-pipeline`
Review commit for new caching logic, data loading, or large in-memory data structures
If memory is growing post-deploy: check logs for cache size metrics or unbounded dict growth
Rollback: `kubectl rollout undo deployment/analytics-pipeline`
After rollback, confirm pod memory returns to baseline (< 600MB)
For caching features: ensure LRU eviction and max_size are configured before re-deploying
Check memory growth rate in logs: rapid growth (>20MB/min) indicates an unbounded cache or data structure
Look for 'cache size' or 'entries' log lines — if count is unbounded, this is likely a missing eviction policy
Identify the cache/dict in code: look for module-level dict or class-level caches without max_size
Rollback the deploy that introduced the cache: `kubectl rollout undo deployment/analytics-pipeline`
After rollback, pod will restart with cleared memory — confirm it stays stable
The fix: add `maxsize=` to lru_cache or implement TTL-based eviction before re-deploying
Monitor memory for 4 hours post-fix to confirm no recurrence
Check recent Cloudflare rule or Worker deploys in the Cloudflare dashboard
Review the nginx/Cloudflare config diff for routing rule changes
If caching rules were modified: verify TTL and cache-key configuration is correct
Rollback Cloudflare Worker: use Cloudflare dashboard to revert to previous version
Clear CDN cache if stale content is being served: Cloudflare Dashboard → Caching → Purge Everything
Verify api-gateway is receiving traffic normally after CDN config rollback
Check Cloudflare dashboard for recent Page Rule or Transform Rule changes
Identify the rule change that correlates with incident onset
Disable the suspect rule in Cloudflare dashboard immediately
Verify traffic is routing correctly to api-gateway after rule disable
Review the intended vs actual rule behavior with team-platform
Re-enable rule only after testing in staging environment
